name: Tara Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union or party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yeah, that's fine. I'm on my days off, so you've caught me at a good time. Just don't put my name next to anything about the company, because I'm still on probation for the bigger trucks.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Understood. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a haul truck at a big open-pit copper mine, the kind where the pit is so wide the trucks look like toys from the lookout. I'm on twelve-hour shifts, four days on and four off, and I start with a pre-start check, walking round the truck with a torch looking for leaks and cracked mirrors. Then it's loading at the shovel, hauling up the ramp to the crusher, tipping, and back down, maybe forty loops a shift. I love the quiet in the cab at night, but the night shifts wear me out, and I'm still slow at spotting under the shovel, so the operator on the radio gets impatient with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that sounds like the world I live in now. The company's been talking about AI for two years and so far it's a new rostering app that crashes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at smoko, which is our tea break, that I told them so. I'd post something in our union group chat like, good, now can we talk about the night-shift allowance instead. People would laugh because we've all been half waiting for the robot trucks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it doesn't mean I'm safe. My contract still comes up for renewal every year, rent on the flat went up again in July, and copper prices go up and down without asking AI. The worry I carry isn't about robots, it's about being junior and the first one cut when the price drops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and try hard to get signed off on the bigger 240-tonne trucks by March, because that's a pay step. I'd keep putting a bit away each pay so we get from about three months saved to five. And I'd go to the union meetings more, not just read the minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relief, with a bit of the usual knot in my stomach. Plain life is still plenty to worry about when you're the newest driver on the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd go to more union meetings. What would you actually raise there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Junior contracts. Three of us on my crew are on twelve-month contracts that get renewed one at a time, and I'd want them turned into permanent jobs. If AI isn't coming for us, the company has no excuse to keep us on short contracts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your partner make of all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev, my partner, is a nurse at the hospital in town, so his job feels solid. He jokes that if I lose mine he'll keep us in instant noodles. It helps, but I don't want to be the one leaning on him.

say: The AI talk was **mostly hype**, and I'd say so at smoko.
Now can we **talk about pay** and junior contracts instead of robots.
think: I'm still **junior**, so I'm first out when copper prices drop.
My **contract renewal** and rising rent worry me more than any robot.
do: Get signed off on the **240-tonne trucks** by March for the pay step.
Build **savings** from about three months to five.
Push at union meetings for **permanent jobs** for junior drivers.
feel: **Relieved** that robots aren't coming, but still carrying the usual knot about being the newest driver.
S0.quote: If AI isn't coming for us, the company has no excuse to keep us on short contracts.
fieldNote: Her worry is **job security** as a junior, not technology; copper prices and annual contracts drive it.
She turns the plateau straight into a **union argument** about permanent jobs.
Partner's **nursing income** gives a floor, but she clearly dislikes the idea of depending on him.

steps.text: Get signed off on the 240-tonne haul trucks by March
Grow savings from three months of costs to five
Raise permanent contracts for junior drivers at the union meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots spreading slowly, that's the bit I'd hear. At our mine slowly means the autonomous trucks they're already trialling on the north pit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the office will feel it before we do, the planners and the people who do the purchasing. Online I'd say if a company saves millions on software, some of that should go into retraining us, not just to shareholders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think it buys me a few years, not a career. Autonomous haul trucks are the obvious next step on a big pit, and they already work at other copper mines. Driving a truck is exactly the job a robot is best at. I'm a junior doing the most replaceable job on site, and the self-driving trucks are already on the north pit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my name down for the remote operations course the company runs in the city, where people watch the self-driving trucks on screens. I'd stop eating out on days off and get savings to six months by the end of next year. And I'd ask the union rep to push for a deal that says drivers get first go at the new control-room jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in my chest, if I'm honest. It's not panic, but it's like watching weather roll in over the pit and knowing you're the one out in the open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marco, the older driver I sit with at smoko, is fifty-eight and can barely use the rostering app. He'd never get a control-room job, and he's got two years till his pension. I'd worry more about him than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move to a control room. Do you actually want that job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I like being out in the pit, feeling the truck under me, and a screen room in the city sounds like a call centre. But I'd rather sit at a screen than be on the dole, so yes, I'd go.

say: The **office jobs** will feel this before the drivers do.
Companies saving millions on software should pay for **retraining** workers.
think: Driving a haul truck is the **most replaceable** job on site.
This gives me **a few years**, not a whole career.
do: Apply for the company's **remote operations** course in the city.
Stop eating out and reach **six months** of savings by next year.
Ask the union rep to win drivers **first go** at control-room jobs.
feel: A **tight chest**, like weather rolling in while she stands in the open.
Not panic, but **dread** about being the junior in the most exposed seat.
S1.quote: I'm a junior doing the most replaceable job on site, and the self-driving trucks are already on the north pit.
fieldNote: She sees **autonomous trucks** as the real threat, already visible on site, not office AI.
Pragmatic gap: she **doesn't want** a screen job but would take it over unemployment.
Her first concern for others goes to **Marco**, an older driver close to his pension.

steps.text: Sign up for the company's remote operations course in the city
Stop eating out and reach six months of savings
Ask the union rep to win drivers first go at control-room jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before I'd even finish my probation on the big trucks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs governments to step in, fast, with a proper wage guarantee for people whose jobs disappear. In the union chat I'd be the one posting links and saying we need to organise now, not wait for the layoff letters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the truck job goes by about 2031, when the robots come, but the clever stuff goes even sooner. The planners and the dispatchers who tell us where to go would be replaced by the AI in 2028, and then the control-room job I was aiming for is gone too. So the backup plan I had in the slow picture doesn't exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the three years before the robots to get a trade that still needs hands, probably an electrical apprenticeship, even though the pay drops to almost half. We'd sit down, Dev and I, and plan to live on his wage, which means moving to a cheaper flat by the end of next year. And I'd be at every union meeting, pushing for redundancy pay that actually covers a retrain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, mostly at night. I keep thinking I'd be thirty, starting again at the bottom, and the bottom might be gone too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Dev the night you heard this was really happening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him I'm going to be a burden for a while and I hate that. Then I'd ask him to help me look at the numbers, because he's calmer than me with money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said an electrician's apprenticeship. Wouldn't robots take that too, three years later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, yeah. But someone has to wire up and fix the robots at first, and I'd rather be near the machines than behind them. I don't have a better answer than that.

say: Governments need a **wage guarantee** for people whose jobs disappear.
We need to **organise now**, not wait for the layoff letters.
think: The **truck job** goes around 2031, and the control-room job even sooner.
My **backup plan** from the slower picture no longer exists.
do: Start an **electrical apprenticeship** within the three years, taking nearly half the pay.
Move to a **cheaper flat** by next year and live on her partner's wage.
Push the union for **redundancy pay** that covers retraining.
feel: **Scared**, especially at night, about starting again at thirty.
**Guilty** about leaning on her partner's wage.
S2.quote: I'd be thirty, starting again at the bottom, and the bottom might be gone too.
fieldNote: She clearly understood the **three-year gap**: her hands-on job lasts longer than the control-room fallback.
Her plan rests on her partner's **nursing wage**, and she feels guilty about it.
When challenged she admitted the **apprenticeship** might not be safe either.

steps.text: Start an electrical apprenticeship before robots reach the pit
Move to a cheaper flat by the end of next year
Push the union for redundancy pay that covers a retrain
Plan to live on Dev's nursing wage while retraining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for the thinking side, and the trucks around 2034. I'd be thirty-five by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing, that it needs a plan from government and the company, but I'd say it calmer. There'd be time to argue about it properly and not just panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means I've got time to do this right. I could finish the big-truck sign-off, earn the better pay for two or three years, and save while I'm still earning it. Then I'd jump to a trade before the robots arrive, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and bank as much as I can, aiming for a year of savings by 2029. I'd start the electrical pre-apprenticeship course at night school in 2027, so I'm ready to switch. And I'd push the union to get the company to pay for part of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious, but it's the kind I can work with. Five years is enough to make a plan, not enough to stop worrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first if you're trying to save a year's worth?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trip to see my sister overseas, which hurts. And probably the new car, I'd keep the old ute with the cracked windscreen going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does five years change who you blame for this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. With two years it feels like a disaster, but five years is different. If people end up on the scrap heap after five years of warning, that's a choice by the bosses and politicians. They'd have seen it coming.

say: It still needs a **plan** from government and the company.
With five years there's **time to argue** it properly instead of panicking.
think: I have **time** to do this right, earning the big-truck pay first.
I want to **jump to a trade** before the robots, not after.
do: Keep driving and save **a year's costs** by 2029.
Start a **pre-apprenticeship** electrical course at night school in 2027.
Push the union to make the company **pay part** of retraining.
feel: **Anxious** but workable, enough time to plan though not to relax.
S3.quote: If people end up on the scrap heap after five years of warning, that's a choice by the bosses and politicians.
fieldNote: Extra time turns her from **reactive** to **planning**, but she still expects to lose the truck job.
Her blame sharpens: with warning, harm becomes a **political choice**.
Saving means giving up a **trip to her sister**, which visibly cost her.

steps.text: Bank big-truck pay until a year of costs is saved by 2029
Start an electrical pre-apprenticeship course at night school in 2027
Push the union for company-paid retraining for drivers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, and the trucks around 2039. I'd be nearly forty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to do it fairly, so there's no excuse for anyone getting dumped. I'd want the union to have a written plan for every driver.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd still leave the truck. Ten years feels long, but I'd be watching the self-driving fleet grow pit by pit. I'd rather get a trade at thirty than at thirty-eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do two more years driving to save, then start a full electrical apprenticeship around 2029. Dev and I would probably start thinking about a house and kids, but only once I'm qualified. And I'd keep pushing for the union to win paid study leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still a low hum of worry. It's like knowing the pit will close one day, you get on with it but you never forget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you have children in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yeah, once I've got the trade. I wouldn't want a baby while I'm on apprentice pay, so it'd be maybe 2032 or so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you trust that ten years would actually be ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Every big change at the mine came faster than the bosses said, so I'd move early.

say: Ten years is **plenty of time** to do it fairly.
The union should have a **written plan** for every driver.
think: I'd **still leave** the truck, because the self-driving fleet grows pit by pit.
A trade at **thirty** beats a trade at thirty-eight.
do: Drive two more years to **save**, then start a full **apprenticeship** around 2029.
Delay a **house and children** until qualified, around 2032.
Push the union for **paid study leave**.
feel: A **low hum** of worry, like knowing the pit will close one day.
S4.quote: Every big change at the mine came faster than the bosses said, so I'd move early.
fieldNote: She **distrusts timelines** from management, so ten years doesn't feel like ten.
Family plans are tied to finishing a **trade**, pushed to around 2032.
Still expects to lose the **truck job**, which keeps her anxious despite the long runway.

steps.text: Drive two more years and save hard before switching
Start a full electrical apprenticeship around 2029
Put off buying a house and having a baby until qualified
Push the union to win paid study leave

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028, because the backup jobs vanish before the truck job does. What would help is the company paying for retraining while we're still employed, and a wage that keeps us going while we learn. Not a pamphlet and a pat on the back.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns the robots. If the haul trucks drive themselves, the profit doesn't disappear, it just goes somewhere else. I'd like some of it to come back to the town that dug the pit.

headlineQuote: If the haul trucks drive themselves, the profit doesn't disappear, it just goes somewhere else.
portrait: Tara is a **27-year-old haul truck** driver on twelve-hour shifts at an open-pit copper mine.
She's **junior** on an annual contract, rents with her nurse partner and has about three months saved.
She's **pro-union** and blames bosses and politicians, not the technology, for any harm.
Across the pictures she plans an **electrical apprenticeship**, leaning on her partner's wage if needed.
She **distrusts management timelines**, so even ten years of warning feels short.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because control-room backup jobs vanish before the truck job does.
whatWouldHelp: **Company-paid retraining** while still employed, with a **wage** to live on while learning.
